verdict: Caution: lend selectively to Kanpur footwear exporters with confirmed NZ orders and clean receivables; avoid unorganised job-work units and retail-only traders.
title: Kanpur Footwear: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
Kanpur footwear runs off leather tanneries around Jajmau, feeding cutting, stitching and assembly units that sell into domestic wholesale and, for the better-run houses, export. **Cash turns on leather inventory and buyer credit, not on machines** — the process is not capital-intensive, so entry barriers are low and the unorganised sector sets the price [10]. That means your borrower's margin lives or dies on leather procurement timing and how fast the buyer pays. When a proposal lands, check the leather-to-finished-goods inventory days and the debtor days separately; if debtor days exceed the credit period the borrower actually grants, ask what discount they are giving to get paid.

## What has changed now
Two things moved in the same month. The India-New Zealand FTA took effect 20 October 2026, removing duty of up to 10% on 181 leather and footwear products, and exporters in Jajmau are expected to gain [1][3]. **This is a real price-competitiveness gain, but it is a demand signal, not yet cash** — no order volumes are in the sources, so collect from customer the confirmed NZ order book and buyer names before you size any limit. Against that, India-wide exports are -3.0% Apr-to-date in USD [D], so the export channel is not uniformly strong. UP GST collections are +14.2% Apr-to-date versus India +6.1% [D], which supports the domestic leg.

## Where to grow, and where not to
**Pursue established exporters with a named NZ buyer and a domestic base to fall back on**, plus tier-2 suppliers to those exporters who can show purchase orders. Peer results support the domestic read: Relaxo's Q4 FY26 revenue grew 8.1% to INR751 crore with EBITDA margin 16.5% [5], and Bata's Q1FY27 net profit rose 23% to Rs 64 crore [6]. **Avoid pure retail traders and single-buyer job-work units** — the sector is inherently competitive with a strong unorganised presence [10], and a rating note flags that debt-heavy players are more vulnerable in a slowdown [11].

## How to grow safely
Structure export-backed limits against confirmed orders, with a domestic receivables sub-limit. **Take stock and debtor statements every month, plus GST returns** — the GST rate cut from 12% to 5% caused downstocking and then recovery in the pipeline [4], so a sudden inventory swing is normal, not a red flag, but a debtor spike is. Covenant on debtor days and on the share of export sales backed by confirmed orders.

## Early-warning signs
- **Leather inventory building while sales are flat** — ask for the ageing and the buyer list.
- **NZ order talk with no purchase order** — hold the limit at the domestic level.
- **Debtor days stretching past the stated credit period** — ask which buyer and why.

Sources say little specific to Kanpur unit-level finances; lean on first principles and the peer and rating evidence above.
watch: Debtor days rise beyond stated credit period -> ask for buyer-wise ageing and hold fresh disbursement
GST turnover falls below declared sales -> reconcile and seek explanation before renewal
Order book shrinks or buyer names change -> reduce export sub-limit to domestic level
Inventory days rise while sales flat -> seek liquidation plan and margin top-up
watch_note: Trigger levels are policy suggestions (analytical framing), not data.
